metal.provenance_bullet:
Apple Silicon model, macOS version, Xcode/Metal toolchain, command line,
  warmups, iterations, median, and variance or min/max.
metal.factor_list:
tile shape, launch geometry, memory
  layout, fusion, barrier placement, dequant strategy, routing threshold, or
  specialization.

metal.store_bullet:
Store raw output under `perf/results/`; copy durable conclusions into
  `perf/optimization_status.md`. Do not commit large profiler traces.
metal.commands_block:
scripts/build
scripts/test correctness -q
scripts/test parity -q
scripts/test mps -q
.venv/bin/python perf/bench_kernels.py --backend mlx --preset quick --kernel <kernel>
.venv/bin/python perf/bench_kernels.py --backend mlx --preset comprehensive --kernel <kernel>

slots.backend-notes:
## Kernel Harness

New kernel ports use the shared harness `kernels/common/cdna3_harness.cuh`
rather than re-implementing the oracle/timing pattern: it supplies fp64-oracle
comparison at `../registry/tolerances.yaml` tolerances, a deterministic host
RNG, wave64 reductions, and timing with median/min/max plus GB/s and TFLOP/s.
`perf/harness/run_kernel_bench.sh <kernel-dir>` runs a harness, archives raw
output with GPU/ROCm/HIP/commit provenance, and emits a pre-filled notebook
entry. Follow the layout of `kernels/pooling/pool_mean_rms_l2/variants/rocm_cdna3`:
a self-contained `<op>.cu` with an embedded oracle and `--bench` mode, a
Makefile with `all`/`test`/`bench`/`clean`, and a `README.cdna3.md` recording
the math, the source ported from, the CDNA3 approach, and explicit non-ports.

Harnesses must be torch-free standalone binaries: kernel objects link system
ROCm 7.2 and conflict with the torch wheel's ROCm 6.4 HSA symbols when
co-loaded.

xpu.provenance_bullet:
Intel GPU target, oneAPI compiler, SYCL backend/runtime, Level Zero driver
  when available, command line, warmups, iterations, median, and variance or
  min/max.
xpu.factor_list:
work-group shape, subgroup count,
  memory layout, local-memory staging, fusion, dequant strategy, routing
  threshold, or specialization.
xpu.comparison_baselines:
Compare against oneDNN, Triton XPU, framework paths, naive decompositions, and
  current XPU kernels where relevant.
xpu.store_bullet:
Store raw output under `perf/results/`; copy durable conclusions into
  `perf/optimization_status.md`. Do not commit large profiler traces.
xpu.commands_block:
cmake --preset dev
cmake --build --preset dev
ctest --preset dev
python3 perf/bench_kernels.py --phase all --preset dev
python3 perf/bench_kernels.py --phase all --preset sycl
xpu.profiler_line:
Use SYCL event profiling, Level Zero tooling, VTune, or oneAPI tools when timing
does not explain a bottleneck. Record the trace path and conclusion, not the
full trace.

slots.backend-notes:
## The Two Gates

No change is a candidate unless it passes both gates in `perf/perf.md`: the
fp64-oracle ctest suite and torch.xpu parity. A speedup that regresses either
gate is not a win.

cpu.provenance_bullet:
CPU model, core count, ISA target, OS, compiler and flags, thread count,

cpu.factor_list:

cpu.comparison_baselines:
Compare against optimized library paths (Accelerate/BLAS, oneDNN where
  available), naive decompositions, and current CPU kernels where relevant.

cpu.commands_block:
cmake --preset perf && cmake --build --preset perf
ctest --preset test
scripts/bench --preset quick --kernel <kernel>
scripts/bench --out-dir "perf/results/$(date +%F)/<label>"
cpu.profiler_line:
